title: Lester Nelson, saxophonist at the Rialto Club
summary: Bergen recalls Lester Nelson from 1933-34, a natural harmony player and tenor man who later made fish-hook flyers.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: While we're talking about different things we didn't get into Lester Nelson very much. He's a guy that I hear people talk about and don't know much about him.

Now we're going back to about 1933 or 34. At the Rialto Club is where I met Lester Nelson. Real good looking guy Dick. On order of Charleston Heston you might say on that order. Maybe not as big. Real fine looking man. He had a wonderful ear for harmony. He didn't read. He was a guy. And I don't remember his, I don't know how he's driving like Murray used to drive on tenor. We call him riding the beat. Yeah. But I know one thing everybody said that he was one of the best team up men going on tenor. And we heard one night at the Woodman Hall we weren't playing. And another guy we heard Harry Shields, Steve Massico and this Lester Nelson. Three sax team sounded like they were reading. Beautiful harmony. Those fellas were all naturals. But Lester Nelson he finally ended up making flyers for fish hooks. He was very famous for that. And then later on he got sick and died. He always had stomach trouble even when I played with him back in 1933 or 34. He had stomach trouble. But he was a good looking guy and he played fine. But he was strictly for a small man.
Who did he sound like as we know through records? Anybody in particular?
I'll tell you maybe my ear wasn't developed then but I never could put him in a category. I don't know why.
Maybe he's original. I don't know.
I don't know. You'd have to ask Harry Shields maybe. Harry played with him plenty.
